newsitem.title: UK: Global bond prospects positive in 1997 - Yamaichi.
newsitem.headline: Global bond prospects positive in 1997 - Yamaichi.

text.p: The market pessimism overhanging forecasts for global bond markets in 1997 may be misplaced, analysts at Yamaichi International (Europe) told investors at a seminar in London on Friday.
Slower growth and the prospects for continued low inflation in the U.S. could cause the yield on 10-year T-notes to fall by 50 basis points over the next 12 months, they said.

In Europe, financial markets are discounting European Economic and Monetary Union starting on time but there is still room for convergence in high yielding bonds as 'possible' EMU contenders near the required fiscal deficit criteria.

"The acid test is that the market got the (U.S.) inflation expectation wrong and something has to give," said Nigel Richardson, Yamaichi's head of bond research. "Inflation has been better than expected and bonds have been too pessimistic."
He said measures were now in place to slow the rate of adjustment to the inflation background which gave scope for nominal yields on 10- and 30-year Treasury bonds to come down.

Yamaichi's overall view is for 10-year T-note yields to be below 6.0 percent and the long bond yield below 6.25 percent by the end of the year. The yield on 10-year T-notes is currently 6.58 percent, while the 30-year benchmark bond is yielding 6.86 percent.

But it is not all cut and dried. There are risks to Treasuries if U.S. interest rates are raised or if the Bank of Japan intervenes significantly to prop up the yen and has to realise its investments in U.S. Treasuries.

In Europe the issue of EMU remains high on the agenda. Taking Eurobond yield spreads in high yielding countries as a guideline, Richardson said the 10-year Spanish Bonos spread against Bunds had the potential to shrink to 40 basis points over the next 12 months as the probability of Spain being included in EMU increased.
He said for Italy there was also the opportunity of increasing spread gains against Bunds, with scope for further interest rate cuts and a reduction in the budget deficit.

"Although Italy probably won't make it (the start of EMU) it is still possible," said Richardson. "We are forecasting a 65 basis point spread for Italy from the perception that they will participate in 2001-2002."
The BTP/Bund spread is now at 151 basis points, while the Bonos/Bund gap is at 95.
For core Europe, Richardson said the debate would now turn to speculation over the post-EMU spread.
Turning to Britain, Yamaichi pictured the year divided into two scenarios, pre-election and post-election.
"Pre-election the market has not fully discounted the prospect of a Labour government...there is potential for the spread to widen to 210 basis points," Richardson said.
After the election, assuming the Labour party were in power, he forecast the gilt/Bund spread at 170 basis points in 12 months, reflecting continued uncertainty about government policy.
Gilts currently yield 182 basis points over Bunds.
For Japan, Yamaichi analysts also saw the market outlook for bonds as too bearish.

Japanese fiscal contraction and forecasts of slower growth leading to a wider output gap, coupled with the possibility of real interest rates being too high and anticipation of a more stable position for the yen, could all contribute to an upward drift in Japanese government bond yields by the end of the year, they said.
